notes:
I found no real disagreement between Protestant traditions on this chapter. The commentators I read mostly agree on the main reading: God reversed Haman's plot, the Jews fought in self-defence, they refused to take plunder, and the Amalek link matters. Where they differ, it's between individual commentators, mainly over the killings (vv. 13–16) and the "fasting" line in v. 31. I ran out of searches before I could read any Lutheran, Pentecostal, Orthodox (oca.org) or prosperity/word-of-faith pages on this chapter, so those are left out.

**Vv. 1–5: the day of reversal**

- **v. 1:** Jamieson-Fausset-Brown say the 13th of Adar was the day Haman's superstitious advisers had led him to select as the most fortunate for the execution of his exterminating scheme. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Est/Est_009.cfm
- **v. 1:** Guzik says the Jews had enemies, but the king and all his resources were on their side. He applies this to believers with Romans 8:31 ("If God is for us…"). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-9/
- **v. 1:** The Light of Israel commentary says that despite the second decree many Persians still attacked, but found the Jews well prepared and armed. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/esther/9-1.html
- **v. 2:** Keil & Delitzsch explain "lay hands on" as a phrase for an attempt to kill (also used in 2:21 and 3:6). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/esther-9.html
- **vv. 2–4:** Bible Hub says the Hebrew word for "fear" (*pachad*) implies dread or terror. https://biblehub.com/esther/9.htm
- **v. 3:** Coffman says Persian officials could see that the king and Mordecai both favoured the Jews, so anyone who attacked them would bring trouble on himself. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/esther/9-9.html
- **v. 3:** Rawlinson (quoted in the Preacher's Homiletical) calls the officials' help "very important." He links it to the objection that the story is unbelievable because it has Jews killing 75,000 Persians. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/esther-9.html
- **v. 5:** Keil reads "did as they pleased" as meaning they retaliated upon their enemies at their discretion. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/esther-9.html
- **v. 5:** Gill, citing the Targum, says some fought with swords and others with clubs and staves. He takes "did as they pleased" to mean the enemies were wholly in their power. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/esther-9.html
- **v. 5:** Matthew Henry says the Jews were strangely strengthened and their enemies weakened, so that none of those who had marked themselves out to destroy the Jews escaped. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Est/Est_009.cfm

**Vv. 6–10: Susa and Haman's sons**

- **v. 6:** Gill says the 500 were killed in the city around the palace, not inside the palace itself. He thinks they were no doubt Haman's faction. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/esther-9.html
- **vv. 7–9:** Henry reports the Jewish custom of reading all ten names in one breath, because they died together. He adds the Targum story that Zeresh escaped with seventy more children. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Est/Est_009.cfm
- **vv. 7–10:** Guzik, also quoting Spurgeon, links Haman (an Agagite) to the Amalekites. Saul failed to carry out God's judgment on them (1 Samuel 15), and Mordecai, another Benjamite descended from Kish, finished it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-9/
- **v. 10, no plunder:** Bible Hub reads the refusal as showing the aim was justice, not greed. https://biblehub.com/esther/9.htm
- **v. 10:** Henry adds that the decree allowed them to kill women and children (8:11), but they spared them. They left the goods so the families could live. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Est/Est_009.cfm

**Vv. 11–16: the second day and the 75,000**

- **v. 12:** Gill notes the Targum adds that the 500 were "of the seed of Amalek." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/esther-9.html
- **v. 12:** Keil reads the king's question as: if 500 died in Susa, how many more in the provinces? https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/esther-9.html
- **v. 13 (most debated verse), defending Esther:**
  - Guzik admits many criticise Esther here for a lack of love. He defends her as following Joshua's principle of not settling for less than total victory. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-9/
  - The Pulpit Commentary grants the request has a bloodthirsty appearance; but, without a more complete knowledge of the facts than we possess, we cannot say that it was unjustifiable. https://studylight.org/commentaries/tpc/esther-9.html
  - The Homiletical commentary says the text shows nothing vindictive in Esther or Mordecai. The Jews killed in self-defence and only killed men. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/esther-9.html
- **v. 13, critical views:**
  - The 1901 Jewish Encyclopedia describes the queen as not content with a single day's slaughter. https://www.studylight.org/encyclopedias/eng/tje/e/esther.html
  - The Bridgeway commentary calls the extra day time to "take revenge." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/esther/9-9.html
- **v. 14:** Precept Austin says the sons were already dead and were displayed on poles as a warning, probably taken down before sunset as Deuteronomy 21:22–23 requires. https://www.preceptaustin.org/esther_8-10_commentary
- **v. 15:** Henry says the 300 had escaped on the first day. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Est/Est_009.cfm
- **v. 16:**
  - The Pulpit Commentary says "rest" seems out of place before the death count is given. Some scholars suspect a copying error or an insertion. https://studylight.org/commentaries/tpc/esther-9.html
  - The Pulpit also argues that 75,800 was a small share of the non-Jewish population, and that probably only those who attacked were killed. Same URL.
  - Jamieson-Fausset-Brown think those killed were mostly Amalekites, which fulfilled Exodus 17 and Deuteronomy 25. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Est/Est_009.cfm
  - Henry says the country Jews stuck to one day. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Est/Est_009.cfm
- **vv. 6–16:** Constable dates the events to 7–8 March and tabulates the 500, 75,000 and 300. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/esther/9-9.html

**Vv. 17–19: rest and feasting**

- **v. 17:** Gill says the date in v. 17 belongs with v. 16. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/esther-9.html
- **v. 17:** Henry notes that the feast was held on the day they *rested*, not the day they fought, like the Sabbath. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Est/Est_009.cfm
- **vv. 18–19:** Precept Austin says cities walled in Joshua's time keep Purim on the 15th ("Shushan Purim"). https://www.preceptaustin.org/esther_8-10_commentary

**Vv. 20–28: Purim established**

- **v. 20:** Bible Hub calls this verse the hinge from a one-time victory to a lasting memorial. https://biblehub.com/q/Why_is_Purim_important_in_Esther_9_20.htm
- **vv. 21–22:** The same page lists the customs (rest, feasting, gifts of food, gifts to the poor) and calls them generosity and covenant mercy. Same URL.
- **v. 22:** Gill says "rest" means they had killed all who attacked them. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/esther-9.html
- **vv. 20–28:** Guzik says remembering God's deliverances is good, because we easily forget his works. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-9/
- **v. 24:** Keil says the verb for "crush" is mostly used of God routing his enemies (Exodus 14:24). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/esther-9.html
- **v. 24:** Gill says Haman cast lots for the luckiest day for himself. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/esther-9.html
- **v. 26:** Bible Hub connects the overturned lot to Proverbs 16:33 and Genesis 50:20 (what Haman meant for evil, God redirected). https://biblehub.com/esther/9-26.htm
- **vv. 27–28:** Bible Hub compares the lasting command to Passover (Exodus 12) and to the Lord's Supper ("do this in remembrance"). https://biblehub.com/q/Why_is_Purim_important_in_Esther_9_20.htm
- **v. 28, should Christians keep Purim?** The Gospel Coalition (Reformed) course says Christians aren't obliged to keep Purim. They should take to heart that God watches over his people. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/course/esther/

**Vv. 29–32: the second letter and the fasting**

- **v. 29:** Bible Hub notes that the Hebrew word for "authority" stresses the decree's strength and legitimacy. https://biblehub.com/esther/9.htm
- **v. 29:** The Cambridge Bible doubts that this joint letter made a voluntary custom compulsory. The verb is the same one used in v. 21. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/9-31.htm
- **v. 31, what are the "fasting and lamentation"? (the main point where commentators differ)**
  - Keil: Esther and Mordecai added fasting within Purim, kept on 13 Adar as the Fast of Esther. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/9-31.htm
  - Whedon: Esther may herself have proposed this fast. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/esther-9.html
  - Barnes: the provincial Jews added the fasting, and Mordecai approved it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/9-31.htm
  - Matthew Henry disagrees: the phrase refers to their earlier prayers in distress (ch. 4). More prayers in trouble mean more reason to give thanks. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Est/Est_009.cfm
  - Gill prefers Aben Ezra's view: just as Jews kept the fasts of Zechariah 7:5, they now chose to rejoice at Purim. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/9-31.htm
  - Ellicott, Cambridge and the Pulpit note the words are missing from the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) and may be a marginal note that slipped into the text. Same URL.
  - The Geneva Bible says the feast was to be kept with fasting and earnest prayer. Same URL.
- **v. 32:** Keil thinks "the record" was an otherwise lost Purim document. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/9-31.htm
- **v. 32:** Henry Morris (in Precept Austin) argues the feast's long observance confirms the events really happened. https://www.preceptaustin.org/esther_8-10_commentary

**Other views**

- **Modern scholarship:**
  - Bible Odyssey says few scholars believe that the book is historical, and that interpreters from the ancient rabbis to Martin Luther struggled with its place in Scripture. https://blog.bibleodyssey.org/articles/esther/
  - Bible Odyssey also says scholars have long looked for some other origin of Purim. It reports a Talmud story in which the link to Amalek (1 Samuel 15:3) is what earns Esther its place in the Bible. https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/purim/
  - The Jewish Encyclopedia counts the decree letting Jews kill fellow subjects as perhaps the strongest point against the book's history. https://www.studylight.org/encyclopedias/eng/tje/e/esther.html
- **Catholic:**
  - The Catholic Encyclopedia summarises vv. 17–18 as Jewish vengeance reigned for two days in Susa. It describes the Fast of Esther and the custom of reading the names in one breath, and notes that the feast sometimes degenerated into excess. https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/purim
  - Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include six Greek additions to Esther. These add God's name and prayers, and they play down Purim. https://wesley.nnu.edu/sermons-essays-books/noncanonical-literature/noncanonical-literature-ot-apocrypha/additions-to-esther/
  - Haydock (Catholic) treats the Greek and Hebrew versions as equally inspired. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/esther.html
  - The Greek version's v. 31 reads quite differently, about a private fast. https://biblehub.com/esther/9-31.htm
